strengths: Rigorous methodology with high-quality face-only counterfactuals from real photos, enabling controlled measurement of demographic effects on VLM outputs while maintaining photorealism
Comprehensive benchmark design with three complementary task types (2AFC, MCQ, Salary) that map to realistic downstream applications, with appropriate metrics and statistical testing
Strong quality assurance: 97.9% race accuracy, 100% gender accuracy, detailed validation of face-localized edits, demonstrates careful attention to measurement validity
Systematic evaluation of five state-of-the-art VLMs with clear visualization of patterns, intersectional analysis, and identification of both consistent effects and task-dependent variation
Well-written paper with clear presentation, effective use of figures and tables, transparent methodology suitable for reproducibility, and detailed appendices
Important problem addressing social bias in consequential VLM deployments; findings show demographic disparities persist even under strict visual control with direction/magnitude variation
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: face-only counterfactual approach is well-executed but not fundamentally new; primarily an empirical benchmarking study rather than methodological advance
Severe scope limitations acknowledged by authors: only 6 occupations, 8 source photos per occupation, limited geographic diversity; raises substantial questions about generalizability

Face-only editing constraint may miss important demographic cues (body shape, disability visibility, etc.) and cannot determine whether biases arise purely from facial appearance or require broader context

Limited mechanistic insight: paper shows disparities persist but offers little explanation for causation; lacks ablation studies, attention analysis, or investigation of whether biases arise from training data, architecture, or prompting
Small model set (5 models, all recent/commercial) and limited task complexity (simple binary/categorical decisions); doesn't engage with VLM capabilities beyond basic image understanding
Task×model interactions suggest findings are not universal; effect sizes sometimes modest; substantial variation limits strength of conclusions
Unclear practical implications: identifies persistent disparities but offers limited guidance on mitigation, assessment of downstream harm, or what practitioners should do with findings
Incomplete comparison with most similar prior work (VisBias); difficult to assess specific improvements of FOCUS/REFLECT over existing benchmarks
No clear articulation of dataset/code availability; some implementation details under-specified in main text

strengths: Well-motivated and rigorously executed methodology with extensive robustness checks (cross-editor validation, spatial robustness, stochastic decoding, expression drift audits) supporting reproducibility and reliability of findings

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 state-of-the-art VLMs with three complementary task families and multiple statistical metrics (pairwise win rates, JSD, polarization indices) revealing nuanced patterns in how demographic disparities manifest

Novel use of face-only counterfactuals from real photos provides better control than synthetic benchmarks while maintaining ecological validity; careful quality validation (97.9% demographic accuracy, edits localized to face region with mean difference 0.141 vs 0.022 outside)

Clear empirical findings that demographic disparities persist even under strict visual control, with substantial variation by model, task, and scenario; thoughtful analysis of distributional effects beyond mean gaps reveals important complexity
Transparent and detailed presentation with extensive supplementary materials documenting dataset construction, prompts, and evaluation procedures, supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited scope significantly reduces generalizability: only 6 occupations, 480 total images, North American professional photo contexts only; unclear if findings transfer to other occupational domains, geographic settings, or image types

Face-only editing constraint is insufficient to fully establish causation—other correlated visual factors beyond facial demographics could drive disparities; acknowledged expression drift rate (12.1%) indicates unintended changes; keeping background/clothing/pose fixed may interact with demographic inferences in unmeasured ways

Weak relevance to ACL venue—primarily a computer vision evaluation paper without novel NLP/CL methodological contributions; while VLMs are important for NLP, this work engages primarily with vision domain, making it better suited to vision conferences (CVPR/ICCV) or fairness venues (FAccT/AIES)
Lack of constructive solutions or root-cause analysis: paper documents problems but provides no mitigation strategies, model internals analysis, or actionable recommendations for practitioners

Task design limitations: salary recommendation conflates visual and textual bias from biographies; forced-choice formats with strict constraints may not capture full model behavior; single fixed prompt per scenario limits understanding of prompt-sensitivity

Reproducibility concerns: custom FOCUS dataset difficult to recreate due to dependence on specific face-editing tools, parameters, and human curation; reproducibility dependent on specific VLM API versions which may change

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing social bias in increasingly-deployed VLMs with genuine fairness implications
Methodologically rigorous face-only counterfactual approach that preserves visual realism better than synthetic alternatives, with extensive quality control (97.9% demographic accuracy)
Comprehensive robustness validation including spatial/framing tests, cross-editor consistency checks, LOTO/bootstrap confidence intervals, and stochastic decoding analysis
Multifaceted evaluation design with three complementary task types (2AFC, MCQ, salary recommendation) providing diverse probes of demographic bias
Excellent transparency with detailed implementation, prompts (Figures 7-10), and extensive appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Severely limited dataset scope (only 6 occupations, 5 race categories, binary gender in main experiments, 480 total images) critically undermines generalizability claims—authors acknowledge findings represent 'disparities under standardized protocol rather than population-level estimates'
Limited novelty: incremental methodological extension of established counterfactual bias-evaluation approaches; dataset contribution is useful but not methodologically novel
Questionable ACL fit—primarily a vision-fairness benchmarking paper rather than a computational linguistics contribution; minimal language-level analysis or NLP methodology advancement

Face-only counterfactual approach has unresolved limitations: acknowledged editing artifacts affecting necklines/hairstyles, inability to control face-context interactions, cannot study many attribute intersections beyond race×gender

Descriptive rather than prescriptive: documents that biases exist (not novel finding) but provides no mechanistic insights into causes, no debiasing experiments, and no actionable guidance for practitioners
Missing statistical rigor in core results: main findings (Figures 4-5, Tables 1-3) lack confidence intervals/significance tests, making it difficult to assess whether observed gaps are meaningful

Reproducibility concerns: dataset and code availability status not explicitly stated; reliance on proprietary face-editing tools; unclear if FOCUS images will be released given real-photo copyright/privacy

Incomplete analysis: limited intersectional investigation, no analysis of model-family diversity (all recent large models), task artificiality (2AFC comparison not representative of real decisions), and limited occupation-specific bias investigation

strengths: Rigorous controlled methodology using face-only counterfactuals from real photographs, advancing beyond synthetic or uncontrolled approaches to bias evaluation
Comprehensive robustness analysis including cross-editor comparison, LOTO, bootstrap analyses, and stochastic decoding validation demonstrating findings are not methodology artifacts

Valuable resource contributions: FOCUS dataset (480 carefully curated scene-matched counterface images with 97.9% quality control accuracy) and REFLECT benchmark with three complementary decision-oriented task formats
Nuanced empirical findings revealing scenario-dependent gender effects, intersectional patterns, and model-dependent disparities with non-uniform directions and magnitudes
Strong attention to reproducibility with detailed methodology, explicit prompts in appendices, quality-control procedures, and quantified metrics
Multi-faceted task design (2AFC, MCQ, Salary Recommendation) capturing relative preferences, categorical judgments, and numeric decisions for comprehensive bias assessment
weaknesses: Limited dataset scale (480 core images across 6 occupations) and scope (occupations and demographics drawn primarily from U.S. sources), restricting generalizability and cultural diversity
Face-editing methodology, despite quality controls, may introduce subtle unintended visual artifacts; residual editing confounds not fully characterized beyond face-body mismatch test (Table 4)

Limited mechanistic insight into *why* disparities persist—paper is primarily diagnostic, lacking attention visualization, error analysis, or investigation of model representations and learned associations

Attribution claims somewhat overstated; controlling for facial appearance shows correlation under controlled conditions but does not establish facial demographic cues as sole or primary cause of disparities

Occupational contexts retain inherent visual associations (nurse in hospital, CEO in office) that may jointly influence model decisions alongside facial demographics, limiting isolation of demographic effects
Evaluation limited to 5 contemporary English-centric VLMs with no temporal comparison or vision-only baselines; generalizability to other architectures uncertain
Weak connection to core ACL/NLP topics—while multimodal VLMs are increasingly used in NLP, the primary focus is computer vision bias evaluation rather than computational linguistics
Some analyses lack multiple comparison corrections despite numerous pairwise statistical tests; stochastic robustness results somewhat limited in scope
